title: Sort Array By Increasing Frequency
description: Sort an array by ascending frequency, breaking ties by descending value, using a hash map and a composite sort key.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an array of integers nums, sort it by increasing frequency of each value. If multiple values share the same frequency, sort those values in decreasing order.

blocks.caption: A custom sort key combines frequency ascending with value descending as a tiebreaker.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (may contain duplicates and negatives)"],["Primary order","By frequency, ascending (rarest values first)"],["Tiebreak","Among equal frequencies, by value, descending"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Sorting by a DERIVED property (here, frequency) rather than the value itself is a custom-comparator sorting problem: compute the property for every element first (a hash map from value to frequency), then sort using a composite key combining that property with a tiebreaker.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The composite sort key (frequency, then negated value) is the same technique as sorting by multiple criteria in one pass, common whenever a primary sort key has ties that need a secondary rule.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture a bookshelf being reorganized so the rarest titles (fewest copies) come first. When two titles are equally rare, the one with the numerically or alphabetically LATER title goes first among that tied group.

blocks.caption: Rarer values sort first; among equally rare values, the larger one comes first.

items: Count the frequency of every distinct value first, using a hash map.
Sort using a composite key: primarily by frequency ascending, and for ties, by value descending.
Every occurrence of a value (including duplicates) uses the same frequency for sorting purposes.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
nums = [1,1,2,2,2,3]. Frequencies: 1 appears 2 times, 2 appears 3 times, 3 appears 1 time.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Sorted by frequency ascending, the order is 3 (freq 1), then both 1s (freq 2), then all three 2s (freq 3), giving [3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2], matching the expected output exactly.
5. How Should We Think?

A direct approach could use a manual comparison-based sort (like bubble sort) directly comparing frequencies looked up from a precomputed map, which correctly implements the ordering rule but is quadratic.

Using a built-in efficient sort with a custom comparator (or sort key) directly encodes the two-level ordering rule: primary key is frequency ascending, secondary key is value descending, computed once per element before sorting begins.
6. Brute Force Solution
Precompute frequencies, then use a simple O(n^2) comparison-based sort (bubble sort) applying the frequency-then-value ordering rule directly.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2)","Bubble sort compares and swaps repeatedly"],["Space","O(n)","The frequency map and the result array"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: A general-purpose efficient sort with the same comparison rule achieves the identical result in O(n log n) instead.
8. Optimize the Solution

Precompute the frequency map once, O(n). Use an efficient built-in sort with a composite key of (frequency, -value), so ties in frequency naturally break by value descending because a smaller negated value corresponds to a larger original value.

items: Sort using key = (frequency[x], -x), O(n log n).
The negation trick turns "descending by value" into a simple ascending sort on the negated value.

10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, bubble sort","O(n^2)","O(n)"],["Optimized, built-in sort with composite key","O(n log n)","O(n)"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Sorting by a derived property means computing that property for every element first, then sorting with it as the key.
A composite sort key (primary, secondary) elegantly encodes multi-level ordering rules without custom comparator logic in many languages.
Negating a value turns "sort descending by this value" into a simple ascending sort, a handy trick when only one direction of sort is directly available.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Sort Array By Increasing Frequency is solved by precomputing each value's frequency, then sorting with a composite key of (frequency ascending, value descending). The negated-value trick turns the descending tiebreak into a simple ascending comparison, giving an O(n log n) solution.
